title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.
comments: 32 pages, 6 figures. A general-purpose and extensible software framework for quantum computing

title: Generalized Bloch Oscillations of Doublon Defect in One-dimensional Antiferromagnetic Atomic Spin Chain under Linear and Quadratic Magnetic Gradients
abstract: We investigate generalized Bloch oscillations of a single doublon defect in a one-dimensional antiferromagnetic $t$-$J_{\rm{z}}$ chain subjected to linear and quadratic magnetic field gradients. By mapping the spin-charge coupled many-body dynamics onto an effective single-particle model, we reveal how the Néel background mediates parity-dependent coupling between the defect and the external fields. The linear gradient induces a staggered potential that splits the Wannier-Stark ladder into two intertwined subladders, producing a characteristic beating pattern in the center-of-mass motion with a subband offset accurately captured by third-order perturbation theory. The quadratic gradient generates sublattice-dependent tilts that shear the ladder into a scissor-like profile, yielding site-dependent beating periods that encode the nonlocal spatial averaging of the defect wave function. When both gradients coexist, their interplay is fundamentally nonadditive: the quadratic gradient breaks the two-site periodicity that forbids second-order linear responses, unlocking a dominant cross-coupling proportional to $B_{\rm{z,1}}B_{\rm{z,2}}$. This leaves distinct fingerprints on the Bloch-oscillation spectrum---a rigid baseline hift of the fundamental doublet and asymmetric broadening of the first harmonic. These predictions are quantitatively corroborated by exact many-body simulations of the real-time density evolution and center-of-mass dynamics. Our work establishes a gradient-induced unlocking mechanism for multi-gradient defect spectroscopy in quantum magnets, offering a framework for probing parity-protected selection rules and their controlled breaking via generalized Bloch oscillations in tunable quantum simulators.

title: Quantum-Memory Forensics for Tampered Quantum Seals: Resource-Dependent Sample Gains
abstract: Quantum seals reveal that an object was disturbed, but not where, with which tool, or when the tool changed. We study quantum-memory forensics for sealed items returning through an untrusted network where one tool opens many. Each seal cell is half of a Bell pair whose partner the verifier keeps in a protected quantum memory, a secret Pauli frame turns any attack into a Pauli channel, and a three-tier report localizes the tampering, learns a hidden-parity fingerprint of the tool and detects a tool switch in arrival order, not necessarily in attack order. Attribution concerns attackers who do not erase that fingerprint, which a random Pauli layer would do cheaply. Each result is stated within one of four verifier classes. For per-unit verifiers, which never couple two seal units and hold no untouched reference, the sample separation is asymptotically exponential, by reduction from a known lower bound for one parity of strength up to 1/3. On ten tampered cells it is proved to be at least \qnProvedUniformMin-fold against non-adaptive stabilizer probes and observed in simulation at \qnEoneRatioFine-fold. Against an implemented self-referencing strategy the simulated gain is about twice the inverse squared strength. The value also depends on the attack: destroying the untouched cells makes the reference necessary, whereas copying errors exposes the fingerprint to reference-free probes. We derive the vault's qubit inventory and simulate a seal requirement curve: ten times more seal noise lengthens the seal's lifetime \qnSealLifeGainFive-fold at \qnSealRhoFive{} times the attribution cost at $r=10$.
comments: 34 pages (24 pages main text + 10 pages supplementary information), 11 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Quantum Engineering

title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation
abstract: Blind quantum computation lets a client delegate a computation while hiding it from the server, up to a declared leakage. Its security definitions cover a single round. A variational quantum algorithm, however, delegates many rounds, and its classical optimizer decides from private data when to stop. We study what the resulting round count tells an honest-but-curious server. For protocols with one-time-padded transcripts and fresh randomness in every round, we prove that the server's best distinguishing advantage over the whole sequence equals the total-variation distance between the stopping-time distributions, so the round count is the only residual channel in this model. We also show that soundness composes as $\delta\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ under adaptive stopping, given a conditional per-round soundness property that composably secure verifiable protocols provide. In simulated delegated eigensolvers for the transverse-field Ising chain, the local Polyak-Lojasiewicz ratio measured in iterations 5 to 15 predicts the noiseless stopping round with a leave-one-out error of 1.7 iterations, compared with 10.3 for a constant predictor. Across 14 configurations that differ in optimizer, stopping rule, initialization, system size, shot budget and problem family, the leakage is significant in 12 and ranges from 0.14 to 1.68 bits, and a maximum-entropy bound estimated on held-out sessions lies above it in all of them. For defense, we show that any mechanism acting after the stopping decision can only add rounds, and that differentially private padding costs the full adjacency radius. A fixed public iteration budget removes the channel completely; set at the median run length, it costs 10% of the remaining energy gap. A differentially private stopping rule based on AboveThreshold protects every pair of instances, but it must often stop too early, which makes it costly.

title: Improved two-way capacity upper bounds for amplitude-damping channels
abstract: We derive an improved upper bound on the two-way-assisted capacities of the qubit amplitude-damping channel with decay probability $\gamma$, given by $\log_2[1+(1-\gamma)\gamma^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)}]$. It applies to quantum communication, entanglement distribution, private communication, and secret-key agreement, and, for every $0<\gamma<1$, strictly improves the PLOB relative-entropy bound, the analytic max-relative-entropy bound, and the optimized balanced squashed-entanglement bound. At high damping, a known triple-rail protocol attains more than $99.54\%$ of its leading coefficient. Our method extends sector teleportation simulation to qubits: phase rotations and permutations give exact simulations within fixed-excitation subspaces while preserving the two-level input structure. We determine the exact, additive relative entropy of entanglement of the amplitude-damping resources and the exact regularized entanglement gain at fixed input population. We then derive explicit bounds for generalized amplitude damping, which includes thermal excitation. Combining the amplitude-damping gain with unital and entanglement-breaking channels gives a closed expression that recovers the zero-temperature result and vanishes throughout the entanglement-breaking region. It improves established benchmarks over broad parameter ranges, while the exact entanglement of the generalized resources remains open. Both results admit refinements under an average-excitation constraint. The bounds provide quantitative limits for adaptive communication through relaxing qubits and show how a sector simulation can remain useful beyond channels whose resource entanglement is known exactly.

title: Controlled Continuous-Time Quantum Walks for Power Grid Analysis under N-x Contingencies
abstract: The combinatorial growth of network configurations under N-x contingencies presents significant computational challenges for power system analysis. In this work, we introduce a quantum algorithm based on Controlled Continuous-Time Quantum Walks (CCTQWs) that evolves a quantum walker conditioned on a contingency register held in a uniform superposition of all x-line outage configurations representing the contingency scenarios. The proposed framework encodes transmission line availability in a quantum register and employs controlled Hamiltonian evolution to account for topology changes induced by contingencies. We develop a gate-based implementation using Trotter-Suzuki product formulas and investigate the associated approximation errors and computational requirements. As a demonstration of the proposed methodology, we introduce a contingency-averaged occupation centrality measure derived from quantum-walk measurement statistics. Numerical experiments on an 8-bus power network under N-2 contingencies demonstrate the implementation of the algorithm and characterize the convergence of the resulting centrality estimates with respect to the observation window, sampling and Trotter steps. Comparison with established classical centrality measures shows a qualitatively consistent characterization of network structure, particularly in identifying the most central nodes. The proposed framework establishes a methodological foundation for quantum-walk-based analysis of power networks under contingencies, providing a starting point for future investigations of quantum algorithms for power system security assessment.

title: Extraction erases the gain: cavity loss bounds dynamical-Casimir metrology at ultrastrong coupling
abstract: Ultrastrong light--matter coupling dresses the vacuum with virtual photons whose response to the coupling strength exceeds that of any coherent probe, yet these photons never leave the cavity and cannot be detected. A parametric drive at the dynamical-Casimir resonance converts them into real photons that a detector can collect. We show that this conversion is self-limiting: converting the virtual photons of an ultrastrongly coupled probe into real, extractable photons opens the cavity port that removes them, so the retained metrological gain is set by the accumulated cavity loss rather than by the pure-state ceiling. In the driven quantum Rabi model the pure-state quantum Fisher information on the coupling reaches $1.7\times10^{5}$ times the coherent baseline; at a cavity linewidth of $246$~MHz, typical of coplanar-waveguide flux-qubit circuits, master-equation dynamics retain $0.96\%$ of it. In a 32-qubit Dicke model the retained fraction is $2.6\%$ at the largest photon basis computed. Eighteen lossy configurations from both models fall on one curve of the accumulated loss, the product of linewidth and interrogation time, which halves the retained information at $0.13$. The extraction cost, not the lossless ceiling, is the figure of merit for any protocol that reads bound vacuum correlations through a lossy port.
comments: 26 pages, 10 figures, 9 tables; Supplemental Material included (25 pages)

title: Direct quantum simulation of compressible Navier-Stokes flow via finite homotopy linearisation
abstract: We develop a direct quantum simulation algorithm for finite homotopy approximations to the non-isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes equations. A primitive-variable formulation gives polynomial residuals in the fields and their spatial and time derivatives, including density-weighted time derivatives. On a periodic grid, applying each spatial stencil uniformly to every factor in a shifted product preserves the dynamics of the finite homotopy hierarchy in an affine linearisation. Because each deformation equation depends only on lower homotopy orders, the lifted generator matrix is strictly block lower-triangular and hence nilpotent. The resulting finite-polynomial solution evaluates the final state directly without time-stepping error, while explicit short-time convergence conditions bound the homotopy truncation error on a fixed grid. In two-dimensional Taylor-Green flow, initial pressure balance removes the leading longitudinal acceleration and delays the onset of dilatational kinetic energy from quadratic to quartic in time. At Mach numbers 0.2 and 0.4, the fifth-order hierarchy reproduces viscous dissipation over a longer interval than pressure-dilatation at the same relative tolerance. We identify auxiliary variables representing the same evolving product, compile the finite-polynomial evolution into logical quantum circuits, and recover a signed velocity Fourier mode via Hadamard interference. Together, the Taylor-Green energy budgets quantify the accuracy windows of each homotopy order, while coarse-grid circuits verify the signed readout and measure gate counts. For higher-order evolution on finer grids, merging coincident stencil terms and combining block-encoded products along strictly increasing homotopy-order paths substantially reduce the predicted normalisation cost.

title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 13 authors
abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.

title: Differentiable collision-model control for multipartite state engineering: reachability, geometry, and preparation cost
abstract: We study a differentiable control architecture for multipartite state engineering in which partial-SWAP collisions, a Heisenberg exchange, are interleaved with layers of local phase rotations. Singular collision angles confine the evolution to invariant supports, impose exact fidelity ceilings, and generate an inverse-distance lower bound on the preparation time nearby. Away from them, numerical certificates show that the sampled couplings reach the whole fixed-excitation sector for sector dimensions up to 21, and optimizations reach fidelities above 0.999 for dimensions up to 1716. At generic couplings the number of rounds needed for a given Dicke fidelity, measured by the ratio of independent phase controls to the projective dimension, is nearly independent of the system size, and the quantum Fisher information spectrum is close to that of a random Gaussian Jacobian. Near full SWAP, a slow-time theory, the sharp form of the inverse-distance bound there, predicts microscopic hitting times without fitted parameters: the distance from the singular point sets the clock and its direction selects the effective control geometry. A detuning sweep along two rays shows that the Dicke horizon follows this law up to a detuning of 0.1, where it is two to five times shorter than at a generic coupling in sectors of dimension 70 to 252, while phase-uniform, random-sign, and Haar-random targets are delayed; beyond a detuning of about 0.3 all targets return to the generic cost. The slow-time value for the Dicke target is nearly the same for sector dimensions from 35 to 252. The exchange graph of the effective theory offers an interpretation of this ordering. Counted in two-qubit gates, generic-coupling preparation is costlier than known Dicke circuits; the architecture offers fixed global couplings, local phase rotations as the only control, and no measurement.

title: Verification and Evaluation of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
abstract: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to $\textsf{QBlue}_{\texttt{BE}}$ by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a $94\%$ gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.

title: Mitigating large circuits with a learned small-circuit mitigator
abstract: Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90\% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.
comments: 41 pages, 25 figures, 9 tables, comments are welcome

title: Small-world networks yield tunable quantum codes at short circuit depth
abstract: Monitored random quantum circuits naturally generate quantum error-correcting codes. We generate quantum codes with tunable properties by implementing random Clifford circuits on Watts--Strogatz `small-world' networks and tailor code properties via three knobs: nonlocal graph rewiring, measurement rate, and circuit depth. On fully rewired networks, circuits of logarithmic depth produce codes with a finite rate and an extensive mean contiguous distance with failure probability substantially lower than codes produced from local circuits. These small-world codes form at a circuit depth growing as $\ln n$ compared to polynomial depths required for codes produced from local networks. Rewiring also moves the purification transition to higher measurement rates and changes its critical exponents. Connectivity is thus a knob for designing codes.

title: Floquet spectra and parameter sensitivity of entanglement in the quantum kicked top
abstract: We investigate the relationship between the Floquet spectrum and the sensitivity of the entanglement landscape to parameter and initial condition change in the quantum kicked top. We focus on the case of four qubits and on locating degeneracies in its Floquet eigenphases using the resultant of its characteristic polynomial $p$ and its derivative $\partial_{\lambda}p$ and quantitatively map the sensitivity of the entanglement landscape to changes in kicking strength over the sphere of spin coherent initial states. We find that prominent sensitivity maxima coincide with either Floquet eigenphase degeneracies or kick strengths exhibiting short-period quantum revivals, with some points satisfying both conditions. These results establish a connection between the spectral structure of the Floquet operator and entanglement landscape sensitivity, demonstrating the utility of the resultant in studying the dynamics of small-$j$ quantum kicked tops. Since this structure extends to all values of $j$, the central lessons apply completely generally.

title: Resilience of Entangling Gates to Spatiotemporally Correlated Noise
abstract: As quantum processors scale, spatially and temporally correlated noise is emerging as a limiting factor in the fidelity of multiqubit gates. Here we show that this makes the choice of entangling operation a first-order design decision: for two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits, the CZ and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates exhibit a pronounced resilience to correlated noise relative to the SWAP gate, even though correlated fluctuations of the entangling interaction can degrade gate performance to a level comparable to that of local noise. We trace this hierarchy to the redistribution of noise-sensitive channels away from zero frequency and show it to hold for noise spectra dominated by low-frequency weight, including $1/f$ and Lorentzian. These results follow from a general expression, derived here, for the average gate infidelity under arbitrary spatiotemporal noise correlations, valid for generic multiqubit systems and system-environment coupling structures. The infidelity takes the form of a spectral overlap between the noise correlation matrix and a gate-dependent filter function, in which the coherent dynamics of the gate itself shapes the spectral window through which correlated fluctuations enter. The framework converts measured noise correlations into quantitative error budgets and provides a concrete design principle for selecting entangling operations in scalable quantum architectures.
comments: 9 pages, 3 figures + Supplemental Material (11 pages, 2 figures)

title: Linear entanglement suffices for $f$-routing
abstract: In $f$-routing, Alice receives an $n$-bit string $x$ and an unknown qubit, and Bob receives an $n$-bit string $y$. They share a state prepared in advance and exchange one simultaneous message each. The party selected by the Boolean function $f(x,y)$ must then recover the unknown qubit without further communication. To perform $f$-routing successfully, Alice and Bob need to share entanglement that scales with $n$ for some functions $f$, but the lower and upper bounds for the entanglement are not tight. This paper shows that $2n+2$ shared EPR pairs suffice for every function $f$. The best previous bound that holds for all functions is a shared state of $2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}$ qubits. The new strategy moves the cost from the shared state to the messages: Alice sends an exponentially long message of $2^{n+1}+1$ qubits, while Bob sends only classical bits. When the messages are counted towards the resources as well, the previous strategy remains the cheapest known. The result also limits lower bounds that count only the shared state: they cannot exceed a linear number of EPR pairs. The result is formalized in Lean.

title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
abstract: Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
abstract: In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

title: Quantifying superposition via coherence by stochastic orthogonalization
abstract: Here we present an approach to quantifying superposition of nonorthogonal reference states through quantum coherence. No change of basis achieves this: every orthonormal basis makes some superposition-free states appear coherent. We show that orthogonalization succeeds instead as a measurement mapping every reference state onto a multiple of a basis vector in each outcome; such measurements are exactly the free operations that convert superposition into coherence. The largest average coherence they extract from a state, which we call its degree of superposition, turns every coherence measure into a superposition measure with the same operational meaning. An interference term becomes coherence at most with the probability of unambiguously discriminating its two reference states, a bound attained when there are no others and, for positive coefficients and nonnegative overlaps, exactly when the overlaps are probabilities of a random grouping. Maximal degree means conversion into a maximally coherent state with certainty, possible for up to three reference states but not in general. Each coherence measure gives its own degree; when two degrees order two superpositions oppositely, neither converts into the other with certainty, and we find such pairs already for two reference states, unlike in qubit coherence. For equal positive overlaps, in-phase superpositions are rigid: deterministic conversions that keep all components can only permute their coefficients. As the reference states merge, the degree stays bounded where widely used measures can diverge, and at every amplitude a rotation-symmetric cat state attains its maximum. Our results quantify superposition operationally and reveal conversion constraints created by nonorthogonality.

title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
abstract: A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $\gamma\id+(1-\gamma)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $\gamma>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4\gamma^2/3$ and $\gamma^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

title: Remote Charging of Quantum Batteries via a Multimode Resonator
abstract: We study the remote charging of a qubit battery by a qubit charger coupled through a finite multimode resonator. The charging protocol uses time-shifted coupling pulses that account for the spatial phases of the resonator modes. We compare the energy stored in the battery with its ergotropy, the maximum work extractable by a local unitary operation. In the single-excitation regime considered here, the battery stores energy at any nonzero excited-state population, but its ergotropy is positive only when that population exceeds one half. In the absence of loss, stronger coupling brings the battery above this threshold earlier, while the final charge remains nearly complete across the coupling range studied. For the parameters considered, qubit relaxation suppresses ergotropy more strongly than resonator loss at comparable decay rates. After the battery is disconnected, relaxation causes its stored energy to decay exponentially, yet its ergotropy vanishes at a finite time while half of its energy capacity remains occupied. For a fixed storage interval, disconnecting at the population maximum therefore preserves the most extractable work.

title: What can a quantum network promise about the entangled pairs it delivers?
abstract: Quantum networks will give users entangled pairs of qubits, the resource behind teleportation and quantum-secure keys. But a user cannot check a pair without destroying it, so networks promise the quality of each pair, its fidelity, from a physical model rather than from a measurement. If the model is too optimistic, the delivery rule alone may miss the error. We ask: what can a network actually guarantee? Our main result has two sides. By testing some pairs at random, in secret, users can put a lower bound on the average fidelity of the pairs they keep, without any model and at every moment. But when they test only a small fraction and keep most pairs, the tests cannot reliably show that every kept pair meets a fidelity threshold: a rare bad pair can still slip through. A promise about every single pair therefore rests on a model, and we give a rule that bounds each user's risk of ever receiving a bad pair under any data-driven routing, as long as the model is not optimistic or a large enough margin is declared in advance. Real data show calibration noise beyond chance, and in simulated networks a model error of the size seen in one experiment breaks the per-pair promise unless the margin was declared. On real data from trapped-ion and diamond links, the number of pairs decided how strong the certificate was: with about 3,000 pairs of a kilohertz link and 20% tested, the median certificate was 0.818, against the 0.817 we predicted in advance. We then ran the protocol ourselves on a 36-qubit trapped-ion processor in 50 pre-registered jobs. The certificate came within 0.003 of the measured fidelity, dropped by the predicted amount when we secretly damaged a third of the pairs, and, without changes, certified three- and four-qubit entangled states. The same tests also catch an optimistic model, but slowly. We pre-registered every confirmatory analysis and report the failures too.
comments: 47 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables. Code, pre-registrations and data: this https URL

title: Local redundancies are necessary for long-lived memories in finite spatial dimensions
abstract: We prove a no-go theorem for exponentially long-lived thermal memories, based on the structure of redundancies among Hamiltonian terms. For local stabilizer Hamiltonians in finite spatial dimensions, the absence of local redundancies---relations in which the product of a small number of Hamiltonian terms equals the identity---is known to preclude bulk thermodynamic phase transitions. Yet glassy dynamics can still sustain long-lived memories even without a thermodynamic transition, as demonstrated by LDPC codes on non-Euclidean graphs. A longstanding question, exemplified by Haah's cubic code, is whether such a mechanism can also support passive (quantum) memory in finite-dimensional Euclidean systems. We show that this route fails for local stabilizer Hamiltonians without local redundancies: at any constant nonzero temperature, local heat-bath dynamics is fast mixing, with $O(N)$ mixing time, where $N$ is the number of qubits. We establish this by proving a strong decay of correlations property of the thermal Gibbs state. We further prove rapid mixing with $O(\log N)$ mixing time under a stronger condition on induced redundancies in suitably chosen regions. This stronger result applies to several well-studied examples, including Haah's cubic code and its generalizations, as well as three-dimensional layer codes. Our work identifies redundancy structure as a key property for understanding thermal memories.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Mathematical Physics (math-ph)

title: Network contextuality beyond binary outcomes
abstract: Can a joint measurement reveal nonclassical behaviour in independently prepared systems that share no entanglement? We study network contextuality by extending the two-qubit test of bi-contextuality [G. Ruffolo et al., arXiv:2507.08461 (2025)] to projective measurements with more than two outcomes. In one laboratory, an observer measures the systems individually or jointly performs two compatible global measurements constructed from them. The individual probabilities constrain the possible classical correlations at each source. For our preparations, every noncontextual model with outcome-deterministic and source-independent assignments predicts a nonzero average product of the two global outcomes. The joint quantum measurement gives zero. We construct explicit product states realizing this contradiction for $N=d$ independent sources, each preparing one $d$-dimensional system, with $2\leq d\leq9$. We derive an inequality in observed probabilities, prove its single-source bounds are exact for these preparations, and give sufficient thresholds for violations under independent depolarizing noise. For this family of preparations the dimension range is sharp: for every $d\geq10$ the individual probabilities admit a zero assigned average, so the certificate fails. The same data admit a noncontextual explanation when source independence is relaxed.

title: Feed-Forward Dimension Control for High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution over Time-Varying Airborne Free-Space Links
abstract: High-dimensional quantum key distribution tolerates more noise than qubit-based protocols, but the dimension that maximizes the secret key depends on turbulence, background light, device imperfections, and block size, all of which change during an airborne or satellite pass. Finite-size security analyses of high-dimensional protocols fix the dimension in advance, and the dimension-adaptive schemes reported so far have been analyzed only asymptotically. Here, a controller sets the dimension, acceptance thresholds, and key length of each block using only public data from earlier blocks. Each block is therefore a standard fixed-length protocol, and composable finite-key security against coherent attacks follows from sequential composition; an inaccurate channel model reduces the key rate but does not weaken security. The controller estimates turbulence from observed error rates, maximizes the expected key under forecast uncertainty, and recalibrates its model online. We evaluate it on a simulated entanglement-based orbital-angular-momentum link between an aircraft and a ground station, using Kolmogorov phase screens and the Hufnagel--Valley turbulence profile. Accounting for forecast uncertainty increases the key by 31\%--47\% relative to a naive planner. Over night, dawn, daytime, and model-mismatch scenarios, the recalibrated controller retains at least 98.8\% of the key obtained with the best fixed dimension for each scenario, while every fixed dimension drops to 73.5\% or less in at least one scenario. Running the link's measurement statistics on a superconducting quantum processor shows device errors close to a constant offset; with these errors included, the best daytime dimension changes from eight to four, and the controller adjusts accordingly.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

title: Interaction-Driven Photocurrent Enhancement in a Quantum Photocell with Opposite Transient and Steady-State Responses
abstract: We study photocurrent control in a quantum photocell with interacting qubit-qutrit donors coupled to an acceptor. We show that stronger Heisenberg exchange coupling and anisotropy increase the transient photocurrent but reduce its steady-state value, whereas the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction favors steady-state output at the expense of transient enhancement. This reversal highlights the need to distinguish rapid current generation from sustained operation when tuning quantum photovoltaic devices. Analysis of donor purity further reveals that the qutrit's local purity tracks the photocurrent trends in both regimes. These results demonstrate that the effects of donor interactions depend crucially on the timescale of operation, suggesting a strategy for tailoring the response of hybrid quantum photocells to different operating regimes.

title: Sharp Purity Based Entropy Bounds and Machine Learning Assisted Entropy Estimation
abstract: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness, motivating the study of its role in controlling entropy variations. A sharp purity-based continuity bound is established for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states. The bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound. In higher dimensions, an explicit sharp bound is derived within the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state. Further continuity estimates are obtained for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families. An application to machine learning assisted qubit entropy estimation illustrates how the sharp bound converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.

title: Coherent Recovery of Nested Codes over the Quantum Erasure Channel Using Erasure Decoding and Quantization
abstract: Motivated by quantum capacity results, we revisit nested binary linear codes for the quantum erasure channel through a packing-covering viewpoint: the outer code supports erasure reconstruction, while the inner code performs erasure quantization. We turn this perspective into two explicit decoder architectures. Architecture I requires no stabilizer-syndrome measurements and combines a classical peeling decoder and erasure quantizer with corresponding coherent quantum reconstruction and cleanup operations that disentangle the logical state from inaccessible erasure-environment branches. Architecture II goes one step further and implements erasure belief propagation directly through reversible ternary quantum gates, providing quantum state healing that reconstructs erased symbols while leaving unerased code states unperturbed. We establish sufficient conditions for exact recovery of arbitrary logical states, and illustrate both architectures using the Steane code, including explicit scheduling procedures and coherent quantum circuits.

title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations
abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) forms the foundation for many logistics and optimization tasks. At the same time, this problem is NP-hard and requires significant computational resources. Quantum computing promises to substantially accelerate computations or increase solution accuracy. The TSP can be conveniently mapped onto the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulation, which in turn can be solved using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) methods, but this mapping requires a quadratic number of qubits. The higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) formulation requires significantly fewer qubits, but it contains higher-order terms. In our work, we thoroughly investigate both formulations and provide a practical recipe for solving the TSP. We give a comprehensive study and compare in detail QUBO and HOBO formulations.

title: Exponential advantage in quantum observation with one extra qubit
abstract: While quantum technologies promise to revolutionise how we observe the physical world, achieving substantial advantages with minimal overhead remains a central pursuit. Here, we show that augmenting a quantum machine with just one extra qubit yields an exponential advantage in probing quantum many-body dynamics. We propose an algorithm that uses this qubit to coherently interfere dynamical trajectories, simultaneously estimating exponentially many multi-time correlators with exponentially fewer evolutions than any ancilla-free scheme. Remarkably, this advantage holds even when the ancilla-free machine has unrestricted coherence time and arbitrary adaptive control, and persists even for a single correlator. We further prove that extending coherence time exponentially enhances observational power, establishing our protocol's optimality in both space and time. Finally, we numerically demonstrate our approach by predicting higher-order probe signals in a many-body system with orders-of-magnitude fewer experimental runs than previous methods. These results highlight the broad utility of our framework across quantum learning, sensing, and simulation.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Mathematical Physics (math-ph); Atomic Physics (physics.atom-ph)

title: Geometric properties of concatenated geometric and holonomic quantum gates
abstract: We investigate the geometric properties of concatenated quantum gates, focusing on the distinction between geometric and holonomic quantum computation. We show that, although individual gates may be purely geometric, their concatenation does not generally preserve this property, since the cyclic states of the composite operation can accumulate nontrivial dynamical phases over the course of the concatenated evolution. In contrast, we demonstrate that concatenations of arbitrary single-qubit holonomic gates remain holonomic, provided that the parallel-transport condition holds throughout the evolution and the computational subspace undergoes cyclic evolution. The preservation of geometric or holonomic character under concatenation is an important prerequisite for extending arguments underlying geometric protection from individual gates to complete quantum circuits.

title: A Frequency-Learning Interpolation-Based Coordinate Descent Method to Optimize Parameterized Quantum Circuits on Quantum Hardware
abstract: Structure-aware optimizers have been the focus of recent study for the optimization of parameters in variational quantum circuits. Many of these optimizers follow a coordinate-based paradigm, making single parameter updates by using classical approximations to the cost function generated from quantum sampling. However, the performance of structure-aware optimizers on real quantum hardware at large system size has yet to be demonstrated. Recently, Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (ICD) has been proposed to unify many of these optimizers into one framework. ICD requires a preset frequency set for interpolation, which can be theoretically derived, but for which the cost function is generally sparse over and may require manual tuning. To address these issues, we propose Frequency-learning Interpolation-based Coordinate Descent (FLICD) to adaptively learn frequencies online, allowing easier scaling up to larger systems. We demonstrate that our algorithm is more accurate than an existing zeroth-order method COBYLA and requires fewer quantum resources than ICD on simulator. Using IBM quantum hardware, we execute FLICD on systems up to 100 qubits and observe robust performance with an increasing number of layers.
comments: Main article: 28 pages and 11 figures. Appendix: 12 pages and 7 figures

title: Constraint-Preserving Quantum Circuit Compilation for Graph Independent Sets via Persistent Occupancy Encoding
abstract: Constraint-preserving mixers for graph independent sets repeatedly evaluate overlapping neighborhood conditions, increasing CX costs across ordered quantum optimization circuits. We propose a structure-aware compiler that reuses these conditions through persistent occupancy encoding. Exploiting mutual exclusion within true-twin classes, our reversible encoding stores class occupancy on the original data register across mixer operations and cost layers. Local mixers are synthesized using target compensation, blockwise parity queries, and coherent restoration; nonuniform cost phases are preserved by an exact coefficient transformation. We prove that the compiled circuit reproduces the original program's unitary action on the feasible subspace for any prescribed operation order and independent layer parameters, and establish exact separability of source-level caching costs under a fixed synthesis recipe. Across 134 evaluation programs and 72 independent confirmation programs, total CX counts fall by 22.61% and 19.87%, respectively, relative to the best of six reference implementations selected per program. Against a matched no-cache implementation, persistent encoding yields additional reductions of 4.10% and 9.13%.
subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE) ; Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

title: Critical Topology: A New Perspective for Phase Transitions
abstract: Critical topology has emerged as a form of quantum criticality beyond the Landau paradigm, challenging conventional approaches to classifying universality classes by introducing topological properties as an additional criterion. Despite substantial progress over the past five years, several fundamental questions remain open. Theoretically, can we establish a general criterion for the emergence of critical topology? Can a unified theoretical framework be extended beyond one-dimensional quantum many-body systems? What efficient numerical methods can be developed to investigate critical topological states in higher-dimensional strongly correlated systems? Experimentally, research has so far focused primarily on single-particle critical topology. An important next step is to realize and characterize many-body critical topology in quantum systems using platforms such as Rydberg atom arrays, superconducting quantum processors, and quantum materials. Major advances in statistical physics often arise from re-examining fundamental concepts. The theory of critical phenomena developed by Landau, Ginzburg, and Wilson, together with the topological phase transitions pioneered by Kosterlitz and Thouless, has now inspired new discoveries in artificial acoustic metamaterials. These experimental observations mark a beginning rather than an endpoint for research on critical topology, and further advances in this direction are anticipated.

title: Where to Hide the Traps: Robust Placement in Verifiable Blind Quantum Computation
abstract: Trap-based verification of blind quantum computation hides test qubits among the positions of a measurement pattern, and existing protocols choose the trap configuration without regard to the delegated computation. We model trap placement as a zero-sum game between a client, who chooses a trap distribution, and a server, who chooses where to apply a Pauli deviation, with a damage profile $w$ and a per-trap detection constant $c$. Since the client cannot know how damage from several positions combines, we solve the game for all monotone subadditive damage functions consistent with $w$ at once. In a single round, placing traps in proportion to $w$ guarantees soundness error $1-c/\|w\|_1$ and is optimal up to a factor $1+\max_iw_i$, while the optimistic solution can fail completely. Over $T$ test rounds, the error decays exponentially against a server that repeats the same deviation, but a general server can keep it at $\Theta(\|w\|_1/(cT))$, and against such servers the damage-weighted placement is exactly optimal. Damage profiles follow from the flow of the pattern: for brickwork patterns with $m=4h+1$ columns, only $(2h+1)^2$ positions can affect a decision qubit, whatever the width. With $k$ traps per round, placing them on this set reduces the number of test rounds by the same factor as for a single trap; with unrestricted trap sets and flat damage we recover the known optimality of fractional coloring. Finally, trap statistics certify the aggregate damage with a number of rounds independent of the number of positions $N$, whereas locating the damage requires $\Omega(N\epsilon^{-2}\log\delta^{-1})$ rounds.

title: Belief-Driven Quantum Magnetometer Control for GPS-Denied Navigation
abstract: Autonomous vehicles increasingly need to navigate without satellite positioning. Magnetic anomaly navigation (Mag-Nav) with quantum magnetometers offers a passive, unjammable fix, but the low size-weight-and-power (SWaP) sensors that small drones can carry are weak, and they are operated open loop at a fixed setting. Interferometric (Ramsey) magnetometers face a trade-off: long interrogation times are more sensitive but become ambiguous when the expected field is uncertain. The navigator's own position belief, pushed through the anomaly map, predicts that field. We close this loop. The filter's predictive field distribution sets the Ramsey phase and interrogation time at every epoch, through a closed-form rule that moves between an ambiguity limit and a decoherence limit. We evaluate it on real U.S. Air Force flight data (real tracks, inertial drift, measured fields, and a survey map tested 18 months after it was flown), with only the Ramsey sensor modelled. Against fixed-setting baselines, 63 of 72 independent flight windows favour belief driven sensing ($p = 2 \times 10^{-11}$). Error falls by 20-27% for low-SNR sensors and 30-44% for mid-contrast sensors. An ablation separates the two ingredients. Phase alignment drives the gain in steady flight, and the rule matches the best fixed setting without the hindsight tuning that setting requires. After a lost start, interrogation time adaptation is essential, cutting median error by 37-42% even against hindsight-tuned phase-aligned settings. Gains are small for high-quality sensors with accurate maps. On an IBM superconducting qubit, the rule's interrogation time stays within $1.3\times$ of the empirical optimum. Coupled with information-aware routing, belief-driven sensing lowers mission error by 15-40%.

title: Spin-controlled thermophase and noise-optimized thermometry in multiorbital quantum dots
abstract: Converting temperature differences into electrical signals underlies both thermoelectric energy conversion and thermometry, which is essential for managing heat in cryogenic quantum technologies. Superconducting circuits typically show a weak thermoelectric response, since their quasiparticle spectrum is nearly particle-hole symmetric. In a Josephson junction, a temperature difference can instead be converted into a superconducting phase difference in an open circuit. We investigate this thermophase effect in a setup where the junction consists of a two-orbital quantum dot with Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Zeeman splitting. A second orbital near the superconducting coherence peaks supports quasiparticle transport over a broad gate range. Zeeman splitting can enhance the thermophase by suppressing pair transport, while spin-orbit hybridization shifts the orbital resonances and can reverse the sign of the response. We assess the junction as a phase-based thermometer using a noise budget that includes readout and current noise together with fluctuations of the orbital energies and the magnetic field. The optimal operating points do not maximize the thermophase but balance a large quasiparticle response against sensitivity to parameter fluctuations. Under experimentally motivated noise assumptions, we obtain projected noise-equivalent temperatures of order $10\,\mu\mathrm{K}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and determine the range over which a linear calibration remains accurate. Gate-tunable quantum-dot junctions thus offer a phase-based route to sensing temperature differences in superconducting circuits at sub-kelvin temperatures.

title: Multi-port few-photon diodes
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 7 authors
abstract: We investigate single- and two-photon scattering dynamics in a system comprising two one dimensional chiral waveguides coupled to a dissipative Rydberg atom pair. By employing the Laplace transform method, we analytically solve the scattering problem and characterize the transport properties. Our results demonstrate robust perfect single-photon diode effects in this system with or without dissipation, exhibiting unity transmittance in the forward direction and zero transmittance in the backward direction. Unlike previous studies where perfect nonreciprocity requires a specific dissipation rate, our scheme achieves this effect without fine-tuning such parameters. Furthermore, we extend the nonreciprocal transport to multi-port configurations at the one and two-photon levels. The system exhibits pronounced photon nonreciprocal behavior in lossy and lossless scenarios, without the need for precise parameter matching. This work provides a robust platform for on-chip nonreciprocal photonic devices.

title: A Fractional Chern Semimetal: Exact Wavefunction and Conformal Criticality
abstract: Unlike fractional quantum Hall states in uniform Landau levels, fractional Chern insulators can host dispersive anyon bands, raising the question of what happens when the anyon gap closes. We construct an exact finite-bond-dimension tensor-network state for a fractional Chern semimetal by Gutzwiller projecting a critical parton state. This state exhibits divergent correlation lengths in charged sectors but a fractionally quantized many-body Chern number of $1/3$. Although it has one electron per unit cell, its modular $S$ and $T$ matrices and entanglement spectrum match those of the $\nu=1/3$ Laughlin state. We identify a $(1+1)$--dimensional $U(3)_1\times SU(3)_1$ conformal field theory (CFT) governing the wavefunction norm in the infrared, an unexpected result for a state with $U(1)_3$ topology. The $SU(3)_1$ sector is a nonlinear sigma model whose Wess--Zumino level and kinetic stiffness are determined by the parton Chern number and Fubini--Study metric, respectively. Under renormalization, it flows to the conformal fixed point, with an initial distance to this fixed point controlled by the idealness of parton quantum geometry. Favorable geometry enables precise agreement with CFT predictions even on narrow cylinders.
subjects: Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el) ; Mesoscale and Nanoscale Physics (cond-mat.mes-hall)

title: A Quantum Model from the Riemann-Siegel Formula
abstract: We construct a two-component quantum model in which destructive interference selects the critical-line zeros of a regularized zeta function within a continuous spectrum. Starting from the exact Riemann--Siegel integral representation, we define $\zeta_{\rm reg}(s)$ by subtracting the contribution of the pole at the origin. The two remaining contour integrals supply the interfering amplitudes. A Dirichlet heat filter suppresses high spatial frequencies, and an arithmetic dressing has a profile generated by prime-power dilations. These transformations map the dilation generator to a self-adjoint, parity--time ($PT$) symmetric Hamiltonian on a physical Hilbert space with a positive metric. Its spectrum is real and continuous. The computed lower critical-line zeros of $\zeta_{\rm reg}(s)$ lie close to the corresponding Riemann zeros and exhibit spacing and pair-correlation statistics consistent with the Gaussian unitary ensemble over the sampled range. Whether every analytic zero in the lower half of the critical strip belongs to the physical spectral family remains open.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Mathematical Physics (math-ph); Number Theory (math.NT)

title: Wigner negativity costs phase-space area: A conjectured refinement of the Lieb--Solovej inequality at Rényi order one half
abstract: We conjecture that the Wigner logarithmic negativity of any single-mode state is bounded by the amount by which the Rényi-$1/2$ entropy of its Husimi function exceeds the coherent-state value, with equality only for coherent states. If true, this refines the Lieb--Solovej (generalized Wehrl) inequality with a remainder term that is a resource monotone, and it implies that heterodyne statistics alone certify an upper bound on the classical-simulation cost of a state. We show that it suffices to prove the conjecture for pure states, since the negativity is convex and the squared $L^{1/2}$ norm of the Husimi function is concave. We prove the conjecture up to an additive constant $\ln 2$ for all states, and identify where the factor of two is lost: For pure states the Wigner function is the wavefunction of a two-mode state obtained by passive operations, and over generic two-mode wavefunctions our constant is already optimal, so that a proof of the sharp bound must exploit the product structure of that state. Finally, we show with an explicit superposition of the vacuum and a distant coherent state that the analogous inequality fails for the Wehrl entropy and for higher Rényi orders, meaning that the conjecture is not a consequence of the majorization relation underlying the Lieb--Solovej theorem.

title: Efficient Shot Allocation and Spectral Reconstruction for Real-Time Quantum Krylov Diagonalization
abstract: We develop analytical and statistical methods to improve the energy estimate from the real-time quantum Krylov diagonalization under a fixed measurement budget. We first express the leading energy variance as a function of the number of shots assigned to each circuit setting, accounting for both the sensitivity of the energy to the measured moments and the correlations among outcomes recorded in the same this http URL use an initial batch of measurements to choose how to allocate the remaining shots. Under fixed-model regularity assumptions, the resulting generalized least-squares energy estimator attains the minimum leading mean-square error (MSE) coefficient within the prescribed allocation class, with the initial measurements included in the total shot budget. Furthermore, we use the same data to reconstruct the Hamiltonian and overlap moments jointly by fitting them to a common nonnegative spectral measure. For asymptotically Gaussian moment errors, we characterize precisely when this reconstruction lowers the leading energy MSE in the case where two linearly independent inequalities describe the feasible moment perturbations to first order. Numerical experiments on spin and Hubbard models show that learned allocation can improve Ritz energy estimates at fixed total shot cost. The experiments also illustrate that enforcing spectral consistency can further reduce the energy estimation error.

title: Liouvillian Quasiparticle Spectroscopy
abstract: Quasiparticles play a central role in understanding closed quantum many-body systems, as they reduce complex many-body problems to effective single-particle descriptions and connect directly to spectroscopic measurements. In open quantum systems, the interplay between coherent dynamics and dissipation gives rise to unique phenomena, such as the Liouvillian skin effect and strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking. This raises a fundamental question: how can the quasiparticle picture be extended to open quantum systems to account for such phenomena and enable the experimental probing of quasiparticle spectra? Here we introduce coherent and incoherent Liouvillian quasiparticles, defined by responses to perturbations acting on one side and both sides of the density matrix, respectively. We propose spectroscopy protocols that couple the system to auxiliary levels, either coherently or via a dissipative pulse, to measure the corresponding complex quasiparticle energies. Numerical simulations of Liouvillians with skin effects validate these protocols, revealing nontrivial spectral winding associated with unidirectional transport in real space. Notably, coherent and incoherent quasiparticles can propagate in opposite directions within the same system. Furthermore, in models exhibiting weak and strong-to-weak $U(1)$ spontaneous symmetry breaking, our results unveil gapless Nambu-Goldstone modes in the coherent and incoherent quasiparticle spectra, respectively; the other quasiparticle spectrum remains gapped in each case. Our work provides a unified framework for theoretically describing and experimentally probing coherent and incoherent quasiparticles in open quantum many-body systems.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Mesoscale and Nanoscale Physics (cond-mat.mes-hall); Quantum Gases (cond-mat.quant-gas)

title: Combining Schrödinger and Heisenberg Evolution to Extend Quantum Many-Body Simulations
abstract: Classical simulations of quantum many-body dynamics face complementary limitations: entanglement growth restricts state evolution in the Schrödinger picture, while operator spreading makes Heisenberg-picture calculations increasingly expensive. Here, we combine both approaches by evolving quantum states and observables independently and joining their dynamics through massively parallel tensor-network contractions. We implement this strategy using tree tensor networks and sparse Pauli propagation, extending evolution times beyond those reached by either method separately in our calculations. For a quench of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model at the critical field, we simulate the magnetization of an $11\times11$ open lattice up to $t=1.20$ by combining state and operator evolution over intervals $t_S=t_H=0.60$. We compare the dynamics with iPEPS, numerical linked-cluster expansion, and X-truncated sparse Pauli dynamics results. We also combine exact state evolution on small clusters with operator propagation on a larger lattice, improving agreement with iPEPS relative to cluster evolution alone. We further derive error bounds showing how the state can suppress operator errors and the evolved observable can reduce sensitivity to state errors.

title: Reconstructing Pure-State OTOCs from Forward-Time Linear Response
abstract: We show that the connected out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) of any pure state can be reconstructed exactly from commutator linear responses alone. The protocol requires no time reversal, no ancilla, no double copy, and no weak measurement: a unitary string pulse, forward many-body evolution, and a single local readout suffice. An average over a complete basis of pulse generators yields the OTOC exactly. We further show that the measurement can be made sparse by restricting the pulses to a fixed operator weight, which turns the truncation into an analytically controlled spectral filter: the deterministic bias can be computed before the experiment and cleanly separated from the statistical sampling variance. For Gaussian states, the finite-weight response is exactly proportional to the full OTOC after a known combinatorial rescaling. For quantum chaotic systems, the typical residual is suppressed as a power law in the sector size. Exact-diagonalization benchmarks in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and a nonintegrable Ising chain confirm these predictions.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Quantum Gases (cond-mat.quant-gas); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th); Chaotic Dynamics (nlin.CD)

title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Ligand and Pose Index Retrieval
abstract: Structure-based virtual screening spans a combinatorial configuration space, motivating a quantum screening framework that targets threshold-qualified configuration indices without reconstructing a complete interaction-score table. Quantum amplitude estimation based on quantum phase estimation (QAE/QPE) supplies finite-resolution phase information to a reversible comparator that writes its decision to FLAG, while optional Grover-style quantum selection (QSEL) amplifies FLAG-selected outcomes and selector measurements identify the ligand, receptor state, rotation, and translation. In an ideal logical benchmark using AutoDock grid interactions as a proof-of-concept model, we evaluated initial FLAG acceptance probability, classification precision, shots required for 95% FLAG detection, and logical Q-operator calls across eight receptor systems and nested libraries of up to 1,024 ligand occupancies. Higher QAE/QPE resolution generally improved classification precision at additional evaluation cost, whereas suitably chosen QSEL iteration counts reduced required shots without improving classification precision, revealing selection and resource trade-offs for extending coherent index retrieval to more physically detailed molecular evaluation models.
comments: 45 pages, including 19 pages of Supplementary Information

title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
abstract: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot. On Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, LoRA reaches 83.9%, tying a 4-shot prompt (83.1%), but generalizes worse to unseen style (48.5% vs. 65.5%) and cuts QuantumKatas from 23.8% to 8.9%; on Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, LoRA beats the prompt overall (92.0% vs. 82.8%) and on unseen style (78.5% vs. 65.0%), and on the 1.5B model as well, so whether fine-tuning pays off depends on the base model, while the Qiskit regression appears in all three. Mixing two replay formats is the best mitigation trade-off (84.4% translation, Katas 21.5%). On 48 parametric functions that must become kernels with arguments -- where executing the input cannot yield a parametric kernel -- models reach up to 83%; on 27 real QED-C kernels, every model scores 0%. Language models can do source-level translation of simple parametric code, but not yet of real programs.

title: Joint Dynamics of Spins and Frequency-Resolved Bosonic Occupations: A Projection-Operator Approach
abstract: We derive weak-coupling kinetic equations for frequency-resolved bosonic mode occupations in the spin--boson model. Rather than integrating out the bath completely, we retain these mode occupations as independent dynamical variables whose equations are coupled to those for the spin observables. A projection-operator construction closes the dynamics on a product-spin ansatz and an undisplaced Gaussian environment with a diagonal covariance matrix. The equations are obtained to second order in the interaction parameter $\lambda$ for an arbitrary number of spins within this factorized closure, and are solved numerically for a single spin. A fixed-truncation calculation using the hierarchical equations of motion provides a benchmark for the spin dynamics with the Drude--Lorentz spectral density. The numerical results reveal a redistribution of bosonic mode occupations concentrated near the spin transition frequency $\Omega=\sqrt{\Delta^2+h^2}$. We also examine the response of the coupled spin--boson system to structured spectra, nonthermal initial occupations, and slow modulation of the coupling. The calculated mode occupations also allow changes in the bath-side occupation and energy densities $p(\omega)\delta\langle N_\omega\rangle(t)$ and $\omega p(\omega)\delta\langle N_\omega\rangle(t)$ to be obtained without requiring an exponential decomposition of the bath correlation function. Its scope is restricted to weak coupling, diagonal Gaussian bath states, and, for time-dependent couplings, the adiabatic regime.

title: Scaling of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence
abstract: Phase rigidity vanishes as a power law near exceptional points, reflecting the coalescence of eigenstates at these points. In this Letter, we show that non-Hermitian skin effects induce distinct asymptotic behaviors of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence. To demonstrate this, we derive exact analytical results for three non-Hermitian chain models and verify them numerically. For the ordinary skin effect, phase rigidity decays exponentially with increasing system size $N$, as the right and left eigenstates are exponentially localized at opposite boundaries. For the scale-free skin effect, phase rigidity exhibits an $N^{-2}$ power-law approach to a nonzero constant as the right and left eigenstates have decay lengths proportional to $N$. For the algebraic skin effect studied here, phase rigidity can exhibit an $N^{-1/2}$ power-law decay to zero, with the right eigenstate algebraically localized near a boundary and the left eigenstate spread across the chain. These findings show that non-Hermitian skin effects govern phase-rigidity scaling by shaping the spatial profiles of the right and left eigenstates, enabling control of eigenstate nonorthogonality without exceptional points.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Mesoscale and Nanoscale Physics (cond-mat.mes-hall)

title: Bogoliubov-picture thermofield dynamics in anharmonic environments
abstract: Thermofield dynamics (TFD) describes finite-temperature quantum relaxation through a purified wavefunction, without sampling thermally populated initial states. For harmonic environments, TFD is typically combined with a thermal Bogoliubov transformation to obtain a compact wavefunction representation. This transformation can also be useful for anharmonic baths, but preparing the corresponding thermal state in the transformed representation poses additional numerical challenges. Here, we explore TFD approaches tailored to anharmonic potentials and compatible with efficient tensor network methods for quantum propagation. We show that the conceptually appealing route of converting a harmonic-reference thermal state into the target anharmonic state by imaginary-time propagation can be numerically ill-conditioned. As a practical alternative, we formulate a multilayer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree (ML-MCTDH) protocol that separates thermal-state preparation from the harmonic-reference Bogoliubov transformation. We prepare the thermal purification in the bare representation and then apply finite-basis Bogoliubov unitaries to the physical--auxiliary mode pairs. For independent bath modes, direct construction of the thermal amplitude provides a complementary initialization procedure. We illustrate this protocol through vibrational relaxation and spatial-superposition decoherence of a harmonic subsystem coupled to a Morse-oscillator bath. We find non-monotonic energy relaxation, shifts in the dominant resonant response, and oscillatory energy exchange at zero and finite temperature. For decoherence, we recover the expected harmonic-bath scaling and find a pronounced non-monotonic dependence of the decay rate on anharmonicity at finite temperature in a low-frequency model, with a weaker dependence in a high-frequency model.

title: Approximation of Semigroups of Random Processes on a Hilbert Space
abstract: This paper develops Chernoff-type approximation methods for strongly continuous and bi-continuous semigroups of operators arising in the stochastic dynamics of quantum systems. The main focus is on applying Chernoff iterations to Markov semigroups of multiplicative random processes on separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The justification of the passage from discrete quantum measurements to continuous ones depends essentially on the choice of topology and function spaces. We propose conditions for convergence to bi-continuous semigroups on subspaces that weaken the classical requirements of the Chernoff theorem. The existence of the limiting bi-continuous semigroup is established in each of the three cases: commutation of the approximating operators, their asymptotic commutation, and uniform convergence of difference quotients over a family of approximating operators. For diffusive models with a generator having bounded coefficients, the derivative of the approximating function is computed explicitly on the subspace of test functions with rapidly decreasing second derivative; the limitations of applicability of this result are discussed. Applications to generalized models of continuous imprecise quantum measurement with unbounded observables, as well as to Poisson and diffusion processes, are outlined as directions for further research.

title: Quantum Metrology With Quantum Limit Cycles
abstract: Beyond nonclassical states, emergent quantum phenomena offer new metrological resources. Quantum limit cycles, in particular, sustain long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation. However, quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving their metrological performance unclear. Here, we propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by introducing nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol.
